corrected_value.title_o: Advertising a Desired Change: When Process Simulation Fosters (vs. Hinders) Credibility and Persuasion

decisions.quote:
In the ninth installment of
Data Replicada
, we report our attempt to replicate a recently published
Journal of Marketing Research
(JMR) article entitled, “Advertising a Desired Change: When Process Simulation Fosters (vs. Hinders) Credibility and Persuasion” (
.htm
).
decisions.reason: The primary source explicitly states that this report replicates Study 2 of the recently published (as of December 2020) Journal of Marketing Research article entitled 'Advertising a Desired Change: When Process Simulation Fosters (vs. Hinders) Credibility and Persuasion.' This uniquely identifies the shipped original (Cian, Longoni, & Krishna, 2020; DOI: 10.1177/0022243720904758) and aligns with blind target_index 0, which captured the identical title but left authors, year, and DOI empty only because the scraped HTML replaced the outbound hyperlink with '(.htm)'.

decisions.quote: In sum, this was an unambiguous success. We of course can’t speak to all of the studies in this paper, but we can confidently conclude that people judge this progression weight loss ad to be more credible than these Before/After ads.
decisions.reason: With the dependent target identity resolved to Cian, Longoni, & Krishna (2020) Study 2 and record type confirmed as a replication, the authors state an explicit overall replication verdict ('As you can see, we successfully replicated the authors’ key findings' and 'In sum, this was an unambiguous success') across both new-sample replications, confirming both main credibility comparisons and the process simulation mediation measures. Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'successful'.

The authors collected new data across two independent pre-registered MTurk samples (N = 761 and N = 769) using the original Qualtrics survey to re-test Study 2 of the published JMR article. Both shipped and blind codings rightly classify this record as a 'replication'.
